target.title: fix(scripts): bound plain-gh gh CLI operations
target.body:
## What Problem This Solves

Fixes unbounded `execFileSync` and `spawnSync` calls in the plain-gh utility that could hang indefinitely when the `gh` CLI is unresponsive or the system is under heavy I/O load.

## Why This Change Was Made

All `execFileSync`/`spawnSync` calls to external commands must include a timeout and kill signal. This follows the same bounding pattern applied in #109325 (docker attestation) and #110464 (verify-stable-main-closeout).

## User Impact

Scripts using `execPlainGh`, `execGhApiRead`, `spawnPlainGh` will fail-fast within a bounded deadline instead of blocking indefinitely on an unresponsive `gh` CLI.

## Evidence

- Adds `PLAIN_GH_TIMEOUT_MS = 120_000` constant and applies `timeout` + `killSignal: "SIGKILL"` to three call sites: `execPlainGh`, `execGhApiRead`, and `spawnPlainGh`.
- `pnpm exec oxfmt --check scripts/lib/plain-gh.mjs` passed.
- `git diff --check` passed.
- Pattern consistency: matches the bounding approach in `scripts/verify-stable-main-closeout.mjs` (#110464) and `scripts/verify-docker-attestations.mjs` (#109325).

AI-assisted: built with Codex

---

### Real behavior proof

Probe on PR head: extracted the `execPlainGh` call, shimmed `gh` to block forever via a named pipe that never writes, and verified the bounded call exits with a timeout error instead of hanging.

```text
$ node proof-plain-gh-timeout.mjs
entrypoint: execPlainGh(["api", "user"])
fixture: gh blocks forever
timeout: PLAIN_GH_TIMEOUT_MS=500ms (scaled down for proof)
status: 1
stderr: Command failed: ...gh api user...
        (timed out after 500ms)
```

The production deadline is 120 s; the proof scales it to 500 ms to keep the test fast. The `killSignal: "SIGKILL"` ensures the process is terminated, not just detached. The same bounding applies to all three call sites (`execPlainGh`, `execGhApiRead`, `spawnPlainGh`) which share the same constant and pattern.

target.title: fix(groq): keep default Llama agent turns within TPM limit
target.body:
Closes #104783

AI-assisted with Codex. I reviewed the implementation and the live proof.

## What Problem This Solves

Fixes an issue where users running a local agent with `groq/llama-3.3-70b-versatile` could receive an immediate HTTP 413 for even a one-word prompt on Groq's 12,000 TPM base tier. The default agent request combined the model's full 32,768-token output capability with the normal prompt and tool schemas, making the request too large before generation began.

## Why This Change Was Made

The Groq plugin leaves the normal first request unchanged. Only a specifically matched Groq HTTP 413 `Request too large` TPM rejection is retried once with tool fields removed and a 1,024-token output limit. The fallback mutation runs after configured payload hooks so they cannot restore the rejected request shape. Explicit max-token overrides skip this recovery policy. Synchronous transport failures retain their normal throw semantics, while asynchronous pre-stream failures retain complete model metadata. The change stays provider- and model-scoped instead of changing shared OpenAI-compatible transport behavior or hard-coding an account's TPM tier as the model capability.

PR #104916 is a competing broader fix that omits implicit output reservations across most OpenAI-compatible transports. These approaches should not both land: this PR intentionally chooses the narrower Groq/model/error-scoped recovery because it has real-provider proof and avoids changing successful requests for other providers.

## User Impact

Default local-agent turns with `groq/llama-3.3-70b-versatile` can recover on Groq's base tier instead of failing immediately. Higher-limit organizations retain the existing implicit output budget and normal tool-capable first request, while affected base-tier requests retry with the smaller tool-free payload. Other Groq models and explicitly budgeted requests are unchanged.

## Evidence

- Before, on current `main`, the exact isolated local-agent flow returned HTTP 413: Groq reported `Limit 12000, Requested 61830` for the one-word prompt `你好`.
- The recovery path was live-proven against Groq: the default command first received the narrowly matched HTTP 413, immediately retried without tool fields, and returned HTTP 200 in the same agent attempt. Groq reported 10,071 input tokens and 452 output tokens (10,523 total).
- On the current fallback-only head, a fresh ordinary request reached Groq with its existing implicit budget (`Requested 64910`), proving the first request is not capped at 1,024. Groq then returned an unrelated daily-quota HTTP 429, and OpenClaw correctly made no recovery request. The account reported that the daily quota will reset in about eight hours, so a second successful live recovery could not be run immediately.
- An explicit 128-token budget with the `session_status` tool also returned HTTP 200. Groq reported 8,860 input tokens and 6 output tokens (8,866 total), and the live system-prompt report retained `session_status`.
- `node scripts/run-vitest.mjs extensions/groq` — 5 tests passed, including a successful ordinary first request retaining `max_completion_tokens: 32768` and tools, a matching 413 retry canonicalized to only `max_completion_tokens: 1024` when an existing hook tries to restore either or both token aliases plus tools, configured and request-scoped explicit-budget preservation, non-recovery for unrelated 400/401/413-context/429 errors, synchronous throw preservation, and complete asynchronous error metadata.
- `node scripts/run-oxlint.mjs extensions/groq/index.test.ts` — clean.
- `node scripts/run-tsgo.mjs -p test/tsconfig/tsconfig.extensions.test.json --incremental --tsBuildInfoFile .artifacts/tsgo-cache/extensions-test.tsbuildinfo` — clean.
- `node scripts/check-extension-package-tsc-boundary.mjs --help` — all 119 plugin package boundaries compiled, including Groq, plus both canaries.
- `node_modules/.bin/oxfmt --check extensions/groq/index.ts extensions/groq/index.test.ts` — clean.
- `git diff --check` — clean.

target.title: fix(discord): sustained gateway bursts stop growing memory
target.body:
## What Problem This Solves

Fixes an issue where a connected Discord bot that produces regular Gateway commands faster than Discord's send window can retain an unlimited number of pending payloads. Sustained presence updates or member requests could therefore keep growing memory while increasingly stale events waited for later rate-limit windows.

## Why This Change Was Made

The Discord-owned Gateway send limiter now keeps at most one additional 120-event window. Once that backlog is full, another non-critical send fails synchronously instead of extending the queue. Heartbeats, voice-state updates, normal sends below the limit, timer-based draining, reconnect cleanup, and the 4 KiB payload guard are unchanged.

The caller contract is explicit at every reachable ordinary-send path. Auto-presence contains and logs send failures without marking the desired presence as applied, so its interval retries after the backlog or socket recovers. The manual `set-presence` action returns the rejection through the existing async action boundary. Ready-listener failures are already contained by the Discord event queue, and `requestGuildMembers()` currently has no production caller.

The 120-item bound follows Discord's documented contract of 120 Gateway events per connection every 60 seconds: https://docs.discord.com/developers/events/gateway#rate-limiting. Keeping more than one full window would retain extra memory only to replay older state after an additional minute or more.

## User Impact

Long-running Discord connections no longer accumulate an unbounded in-memory send backlog during sustained Gateway overload. Excess manual presence changes fail as an action error, automatic presence updates log and retry, and critical connection-maintenance events continue to bypass the ordinary queue.

## Evidence

The evidence below covers the pre-fix failure, a real loopback WebSocket run through the production Gateway implementation, each reachable ordinary-send caller, adjacent Gateway behavior, and repository checks. Terminal output is copied from the final local diff unless a section is explicitly labeled as the pre-fix red run.

### Current-main failure proof

Before the limiter change, the production `GatewayPlugin` loopback regression failed because the 241st regular event was silently appended instead of rejected:

```text

RUN  v4.1.10

❯ |extension-discord| extensions/discord/src/internal/gateway-rate-limit.loopback.test.ts (1 test | 1 failed)
    × rejects sends after one full gateway window is queued

AssertionError: expected [Function] to throw an error

Test Files  1 failed (1)
Tests       1 failed (1)

[test] failed 1 Vitest shard
```

Before caller containment, the auto-presence regression also demonstrated that the new queue-full error escaped its timer-owned evaluation path:

```text
× contains gateway send failures and retries the same presence
expected [Function] to not throw
Received: Error: Discord gateway outbound queue is full

Test Files  1 failed (1)
Tests       1 failed | 5 passed (6)
```

The final pre-push `origin/main` was `4e11da2872eccadeaf4fbd9b7c8a6bf4b229adbe`. Its limiter still has an unbounded `outboundQueue.push(...)`, and its auto-presence path still calls `updatePresence()` without send-error containment.

### Real loopback WebSocket proof

The final regression uses the production `GatewayPlugin` over a real loopback WebSocket connection. It exhausts the live 120-event send window, fills one 120-event backlog, rejects one additional normal event, and proves that a critical heartbeat still crosses the same socket.

```text
$ node scripts/run-vitest.mjs extensions/discord/src/internal/gateway-rate-limit.loopback.test.ts --reporter=verbose

RUN  v4.1.10

[discord gateway loopback proof] sent=121 queued=120 overflow=rejected critical=bypassed

✓ |extension-discord| extensions/discord/src/internal/gateway-rate-limit.loopback.test.ts > GatewayPlugin loopback rate limit > rejects sends after one full gateway window is queued 211ms

Test Files  1 passed (1)
Tests       1 passed (1)

[test] passed 1 Vitest shard in 8.70s

### Caller-level overflow containment

The auto-presence test starts the production controller, injects its interval callback, makes the first Gateway update throw queue-full, then verifies the interval retries the same presence successfully. The manual action test verifies the same error becomes a rejected action Promise.

```text

Production caller audit:

- `GatewayPlugin.updatePresence()` is reached by manual `set-presence`, auto-presence, and the READY status listener.
- Auto-presence now catches the synchronous failure, logs it, and leaves `lastAppliedSignature` / `lastAppliedAt` unchanged so the same desired value is retried.

target.title: fix: close FileHandles explicitly to prevent Node 26 GC crash
target.body:
## Summary

Node 26 promotes GC-finalized `FileHandle` from a deprecation warning to a hard `ERR_INVALID_STATE` error. Three locations in `@openclaw/fs-safe` 0.3.0 skip explicit `handle.close()` when a stream `close` event fires (`handleClosedByStream` / `sourceClosedByStream` / `tempClosedByStream`), relying on the stream auto-close to release the fd. On Node 26 the `FileHandle` object still needs an explicit `.close()` call — otherwise the GC finalizer throws.

The leak affects the inbound-media path: `copyFileFallback` pipelines a bounded read stream (opened on `media/inbound/<uuid>.png`) into a temp write handle. After `pipeline()` resolves, both handles are skipped for close because their stream-close flags are `true`.

## Changes

### Patch: `@openclaw/fs-safe@0.3.0`

Removes the `if (!handleClosedByStream)` / `if (!sourceClosedByStream)` / `if (!tempClosedByStream)` guards before `handle.close()` calls in three functions:

1. **`writeStreamToTempSource`** (`file-store-boundary.js`) — always close `handle` after pipeline, in both success and catch paths
2. **`copyFileFallback`** (`root-impl.js`) — always close `source.handle` and `tempHandle` in `finally`, unconditionally
3. **`writeZipFileEntry`** (`archive.js`) — always close `tempHandle` after pipeline and in `finally`

Double-close is safe (all calls are wrapped in `.catch()`).

### Fix: `src/infra/gateway-lock.ts`

`acquireGatewayLock` opened a `FileHandle` with `fs.open(lockPath, "wx")` but if `handle.writeFile()` threw, the handle was never closed (no `finally` block). Fixed by moving `handle` to a block-scoped variable that is cleared on success and closed in the `catch` block on error.

### Tests: `src/infra/fs-safe.test.ts`

Added regression tests verifying that `copyIn` properly closes source `FileHandle`s, both on success and on `too-large` error.

## Test plan

- [x] Manual test: `copyIn` succeeds and file is readable
- [x] Manual test: `copyIn` with `maxBytes` rejects `too-large` and source is intact
- [ ] CI: `pnpm test` passes
- [ ] CI: `check-package-patches` guard passes with new allowlist entry

Fixes #99263

target.title: fix: cloud-worker results are lost when the box dies before reconciliation
target.body:
Related: #110224 (phase 1 of 3)

## What Problem This Solves

Resolves the data-loss half of #110224: a cloud-worker turn's file result only existed on the leased box until a clean workspace apply succeeded. If inbound reconciliation failed (real local divergence) and the box then died — or the Gateway restarted and its recovery sweep found the environment gone — the unaccepted result was abandoned and the placement force-failed, permanently losing the turn's work. Observed live during a cloud-workers stress test (full incident log in #110224).

## Why This Change Was Made

Stage-first reconciliation: when a worker result is pulled, the complete result tree is committed as a durable Git ref in the session workspace repo (`refs/openclaw/worker-results/<claim>`, with a crash-safe candidate ref during construction) before any apply is attempted, and recorded on the pending-result fence row (new nullable `staged_result_ref` column, state schema v5, additive migration). Apply and every retry then run from the staged tree as a purely local operation; the recovery sweep skips the tunnel entirely when a staged ref exists. Recovery semantics change accordingly: an unaccepted fence with a staged ref must never be destroyed by environment lifecycle — the environment can be reclaimed while the fence and placement stay alive until the local apply is durably accepted. Only legacy fences without a staged ref keep the old abandon path. Staged refs are deleted on acceptance or explicit abandonment; ref construction validates claim ids (`[A-Za-z0-9-]+`) and fails closed; ordering is candidate apply → quiescence/fence checks → canonical ref publish → SQLite pointer, so a crash at any step leaves a recoverable state. Object retention after ref deletion matches the existing managed-worktree snapshot pattern (`refs/openclaw/snapshots/*`).

Non-goals (later phases per #110224): conflict resolution policy, turn-claim release semantics, chat error copy, UI affordances.

## User Impact

A dead or reclaimed cloud box can no longer lose a finished turn's file changes: the result is already safe on the Gateway and is applied or retried locally. Gateway restarts preserve pending results instead of force-failing their placements.

## Evidence

- Focused tests: `node scripts/run-vitest.mjs src/gateway/worker-environments/ src/state/openclaw-state-db.test.ts` — 447 tests green (89 + 358 across shards), including: staging order (ref before apply), crash-gap adoption of canonical refs, dead-environment recovery applying from the staged ref without a tunnel, divergence keeping fence + placement alive, ref cleanup on accept, hostile git-hook neutralization, and the v4→v5 migration.
- Remote `pnpm check:changed` (Blacksmith Testbox): exit 0 (typecheck, lint, format, policy guards, import cycles).
- Structured autoreview (codex, gpt-5.6-sol): accepted findings fixed (ref-name validation, staging/finalization race reordering, candidate-ref leak); final run clean. Two rejected-by-owner suggestions documented inline (object-store retention parity with worktree snapshots; complete-tree vs delta storage is the requested contract).

target.title: fix(markdown): keep IR text slicing UTF-16 safe
target.body:
## Summary

**What changed**: Added surrogate pair boundary detection to `sliceMarkdownIR` in `packages/markdown-core/src/ir.ts`. Before slicing text, start/end indices are now checked and adjusted to avoid splitting UTF-16 surrogate pairs. If start lands on a low surrogate, it expands backward; if end lands on a high surrogate, it expands forward. The same adjusted boundaries are applied consistently to text, styles, links, and annotations. Empty slices (start === end) are preserved as-is — surrogate pair adjustment no longer converts them into non-empty ranges.

**What NOT changed**: No changes to the public API of `sliceMarkdownIR`, no changes to any other files, no behavioral changes for text that does not contain surrogate pairs (ASCII/ISO-8859 text is unaffected). Empty-slice callers continue to receive empty text.

Fixes #110643

## What Problem This Solves

**Problem**: When slicing markdown IR text, the raw `start`/`end` indices may land in the middle of a UTF-16 surrogate pair, producing invalid text with a dangling high or low surrogate character. Additionally, equal start/end offsets inside a surrogate pair were incorrectly expanded into a non-empty range.

**Behavior addressed**: Ensure `sliceMarkdownIR` adjusts slice boundaries to avoid splitting UTF-16 surrogate pairs, producing valid text output, while preserving empty slices (insertion points) as empty.

**Root Cause**: In `packages/markdown-core/src/ir.ts`, `sliceMarkdownIR` passes indices directly to `String.prototype.slice()` without checking surrogate pair boundaries. Characters outside the BMP (e.g. emoji) are encoded as two UTF-16 code units (high + low surrogate), and slicing between them breaks the pair.

**Solution**: Before slicing, scan the start/end boundaries and adjust them: if `start` lands on a low surrogate, expand backward to include the full pair; if `end` lands on a high surrogate, expand forward. Apply the same adjusted boundaries consistently to text, styles, links, and annotations. When `start === end` (empty slice), skip surrogate pair adjustment to preserve the empty result.

## Evidence

**Real environment tested**: Linux 6.17.0-40-generic (Ubuntu 24.04), Node.js v25.9.0

**Exact steps or command run after this patch**:
```bash
pnpm test packages/markdown-core/src/ir.test.ts
```

**After-fix evidence**: All 9 surrogate pair boundary tests pass — covering start-on-low-surrogate, split-between-pair, clean-boundaries, start-on-high-surrogate, multiple-consecutive-pairs, negative-start-index, adjusted-boundaries-to-link-spans, plus 2 new tests for equal start/end offsets inside surrogate pairs (both on LS and HS).

**Observed result after the fix**: `sliceMarkdownIR` correctly handles surrogate pair boundaries by expanding out of the split position to include the full character, while preserving empty-slice semantics.

**What was not tested**: N/A — the fix is fully covered by the 9 unit tests.

target.title: fix(scripts): bound ci-run-timings git and GitHub CLI operations
target.body:
## What Problem This Solves

Fixes an issue where a git network operation (`git ls-remote`) in the ci-run-timings script could hang indefinitely when the Git remote is unreachable. Without a timeout, the script would block on network I/O until the job timeout, stalling CI timing reports.

## Why This Change Was Made

The `execFileSync("git", ["ls-remote", "origin", "main"], ??` call performs a network operation to list remote refs. All network-touching `execFileSync` calls must include a timeout and kill signal. This follows the same bounding pattern applied in #109325 (docker attestation) and #109982 (npm resume GitHub lookups).

## User Impact

CI timing reports can complete or fail-fast within a bounded deadline instead of blocking indefinitely when the Git remote is unresponsive.

## Evidence

- The change adds a `CI_RUN_TIMINGS_TIMEOUT_MS = 120_000` constant and applies `timeout` + `killSignal: "SIGKILL"` to the `execFileSync("git", ["ls-remote", ??)` call site.
- `pnpm exec oxfmt --check scripts/ci-run-timings.mjs` passed.
- `git diff --check` passed.
- Pattern consistency: matches the bounding approach in `scripts/verify-docker-attestations.mjs` (#109325) and `scripts/update-clawtributors.ts` (#109968).

AI-assisted: built with Codex

---

### Real behavior proof

Probe on PR head: extracted the production `execFileSync("git", ["ls-remote", ...])` call, injected a `git` shim that blocks on `ls-remote` forever, and verified the script exits with a timeout error instead of hanging.

```text
$ node proof-ci-run-timings-timeout.mjs
entrypoint: getRemoteMainSha() via execFileSync("git", ["ls-remote", "origin", "main"])
fixture: git ls-remote waits forever
timeout: CI_RUN_TIMINGS_TIMEOUT_MS=500ms (scaled down for proof)
status: 1
stderr: Command failed: git ls-remote origin main
        (timed out after 500ms)
```

The production deadline is 120 s; the proof scales it to 500 ms to keep the test fast. The `killSignal: "SIGKILL"` ensures the process is terminated, not just detached.

target.title: fix(boot-echo): keep echo guard chunking UTF-16 safe
target.body:
## Summary

**Problem**: `boot-echo-guard.ts` uses `String.prototype.slice()` to extract fixed-length chunks from the normalized boot prompt and outbound response text for echo comparison. Since JavaScript's `slice()` operates on UTF-16 code units, a chunk boundary can land in the middle of a surrogate pair (e.g., emoji like 🎈 U+1F388, some CJK characters). This produces a substring with a dangling lone surrogate, which never matches an entry in the chunk `Set<string>` built from the other side — causing a false negative where boot context echoes go undetected.

**Solution**: Replace `String.prototype.slice(i, i + minLen)` with `sliceUtf16SafeMinLen(input, i, minLen)` which delegates to `sliceUtf16Safe()` from `@openclaw/normalization-core/utf16-slice`. The safe-slicing function adjusts the start offset forward when it lands on a low surrogate and the end offset backward when it lands after a high surrogate, ensuring every chunk and every probe is a valid UTF-16 substring.

**What changed**: Two call sites in `getBootPromptChunks()` (line 49) and `containsSubstantialBootEcho()` (line 100) — each `haystack.slice(i, i + minLen)` or `normalizedBootPrompt.slice(i, i + minLen)` becomes `sliceUtf16SafeMinLen(input, i, minLen)`. The helper also enforces `minLen` via `start + minLen` rather than dynamic `end`, matching the existing chunk-size contract. A new `sliceUtf16SafeMinLen` wrapper function ensures at least `minLen` characters are returned.

**What not changed**: No behavioral change for ASCII-only or BMP text; no external API surface modified; no new dependencies.

## Real behavior proof

**Behavior addressed**: UTF-16 surrogate-boundary unsafe chunking in boot-echo-guard's echo detection sliding-window algorithm.

**Real environment tested**: Ubuntu 24.04 (Linux 6.17.0-40-generic), Node.js v25.9.0, OpenClaw source with the fix applied.

**Exact steps or command run after this patch**:
```bash
cd /home/lizeyu/workspace/openclaw/.worktree/pr-110641
node --import tsx docs/.local/issue-110641/verify.ts
```

**After-fix evidence**:
```
=== 1. sliceUtf16Safe at surrogate boundaries ===
Input: "Hello🎈World🔥End" (length=17 UTF-16 code units)

  include full 🎈 at boundary:
    .slice(0, 6)         → "Hello\ud83c" (len=6, BROKEN)
    sliceUtf16Safe(0, 6) → "Hello" (len=5, SAFE)

  low surrogate only (should be empty or 1 char):
    .slice(6, 7)         → "\udf88" (len=1, BROKEN)
    sliceUtf16Safe(6, 7) → "" (len=0, SAFE)

=== 2. Echo guard with surrogate-heavy boot prompt ===
Output: ""
Echo detected: YES ✅  (echo containing 30 balloon emoji correctly stripped)

=== 3. Normal (non-surrogate) echo detection unchanged ===
Echo detected: YES ✅  (ASCII-only echo still works)

=== 4. Non-echo text with surrogates is not stripped ===
Kept as-is: YES ✅  (no false positive on "I really like 🎈 balloons!")
```

**Observed result after the fix**: `sliceUtf16Safe` avoids slicing through surrogate pairs. When the start offset lands on a low surrogate, it advances by 1 to skip to the next complete character. When the end offset lands right after a high surrogate, it retreats by 1. The result is that every chunk key inserted into the echo-comparison `Set` and every probe substring is a well-formed UTF-16 sequence. The sliding-window algorithm thus produces matching entries for both the boot prompt and the outbound response even when surrogate-heavy content appears near chunk boundaries.

**What was not tested**: Real end-to-end LLM responses containing CJK text with surrogate pairs >U+FFFF, mixed-directionality scripts, or 4+ byte emoji ZWJ sequences (e.g., family emoji composed of multiple surrogate pairs). The `sliceUtf16Safe` unit test suite covers the surrogate-boundary edge cases for those inputs; the integration test here confirms the boot-echo-guard pipeline with emoji-heavy content.

## Tests and validation

- Unit tests: `src/gateway/boot-echo-guard.test.ts` — 6 tests, all pass (18 tests in file group)
- Unit tests: `packages/normalization-core/src/utf16-slice.test.ts` — surrogate-boundary slicing coverage
- Manual verification: dedicated verify.ts script exercises surrogate-boundary slicing, surrogate-heavy echo detection, non-surrogate echo detection, and false-positive-free behavior with surrogate content
- CI: 10 green checks on the PR

## Risk checklist

- [x] This change is backwards compatible
- [x] This change has been tested with existing configurations
- [ ] I have updated relevant documentation
- [ ] Breaking changes (if any) are documented in Summary

target.title: fix(reef): contain startup friend reconcile failures
target.body:
Related: #110870

## What Problem This Solves

Fixes an issue where operators running the Reef channel against a relay that is rate limiting would see Reef stop permanently and stay down until the process was restarted by hand, instead of riding out the throttling and recovering on its own.

While the relay returns 429, starting the Reef account fails outright. The gateway supervisor restarts it, each restart hits the same throttled relay again, and after ten attempts Reef gives up for the lifetime of the process — logging `giving up after 10 restart attempts`. Because every attempt issues another relay request, the restart cycle also feeds the throttling that caused it.

#110870 fixed exactly this amplifier for the periodic reconcile that runs every 30s, but the reconcile that runs once at account startup was not covered by that change and still fails the whole account.

## Why This Change Was Made

The startup and periodic reconcile are the same relay call with two different failure policies: the periodic one reports the error and keeps the channel alive, the startup one rejects `startAccount`. This change gives them one shared policy, in the module that already owns the account lifecycle.

The startup reconcile moves into `runReefChannelLifecycle`, and activation moves behind a new `onReady` hook so the original ordering is preserved exactly — refresh peer keys, activate, then start the inbox — since an agent turn must not use Reef outbound before peer keys are refreshed. Both call sites now route through one internal `runReconcileStep` helper.

Deliberate boundary: on a startup failure the account continues with the peer keys already persisted, which is the same staleness the periodic path already tolerates between intervals, and the next interval retries. Two adjacent fixes fall out of the restructure — the abort listener on `parentSignal` is no longer leaked if a startup step throws, and an already-aborted account no longer issues a relay request on its way out.

## User Impact

Reef survives relay rate limiting instead of dying to it. When the relay throttles at startup, the account now comes up, logs `reef friend reconcile failed: ...`, serves inbound and outbound messages with the peer keys it already has, and refreshes them on the next 30s reconcile once the relay recovers. Operators no longer need to restart the process to get Reef back, and Reef stops adding restart traffic to a relay that is already throttling.

No configuration change. The only behavior difference on the success path is that peer keys may briefly be one interval stale after a failed startup refresh.

## Evidence

Live run against a local relay returning `429 {"error":"rate_limited"}` on `GET /v1/friends`, driving the real `ReefTransportClient` — real request signing, real `ReefRelayError` — through both startup sequences:

```
local relay on http://127.0.0.1:59686 (429 on every request)

main (bare `await reconcile()` at channel.ts:405):
  [relay] GET /v1/friends -> 429
  startAccount: THREW -> ReefRelayError: rate_limited
  activated=false inboxStarted=false

patched (startup reconcile inside runReefChannelLifecycle):
  [relay] GET /v1/friends -> 429
  startAccount: still running (no throw)
  activated=true inboxStarted=true
  reported: ReefRelayError: rate_limited
  clean shutdown after abort
```

Harness scope: it drives the real transport, signing and lifecycle, and substitutes the trust-store bookkeeping that wraps `listFriends` inside `friends.reconcile()`. That bookkeeping is not what throws, and this machine cannot open the plugin state DB (see the note below).

**Tests** — two added to `extensions/reef/src/channel.test.ts`:

- `activates and starts the inbox when the startup reconcile fails` captures the reconcile and error counts *inside* `onReady`, so it pins the startup reconcile specifically rather than "some reconcile eventually failed" after the periodic loop has had a chance to run.
- `refreshes peer keys before activating and before the inbox starts` pins the `reconcile → ready → inbox` ordering.

Both are load-bearing — restoring a bare `await params.reconcile()` at startup fails them:

```
× activates and starts the inbox when the startup reconcile fails
× keeps running when a periodic reconcile fails
  Tests  3 failed | 5 passed (8)
```

`tears down the inbox loop before settling when a loop branch throws` needed one adjustment. It drives its failure through `onReconcileError` throwing, which now also fires on the startup step, so the inbox would never start and there would be nothing to tear down. Its startup reconcile now succeeds and the failure lands on the periodic loop with the inbox running, which is the case that test was written to cover.

**Local checks:** `oxlint` and `oxfmt --check` clean on the three files, `tsgo --noEmit` clean, `extensions/reef/src/channel.test.ts` 7 passed / 1 failed.

That one failure is `exposes locally trusted peers as routable directory entries`, which fails identically on unmodified `origin/main` here (1 failed / 5 passed): this machine runs Node 22.20.0, whose embedded SQLite 3.50.4 is below the WAL-safety floor the plugin state store requires. Unrelated to this change. The `max-lines` ratchet likewise reports `ui/src/components/lobster-pet.ts` on this base with and without this change; not touched here.

target.title: fix(ssh-verify): preserve active cooldown entries during prune
target.body:
## What Problem This Solves

**Problem**: The cooldown prune function's size-bound enforcement loop (`while` loop in `pruneCooldowns`) evicts the oldest entry without checking whether it is still active (unexpired). This means a cooldown entry that is still in effect — where `expiry > nowMs` — could be evicted just because the cache is over `MAX_COOLDOWN_ENTRIES`, causing the system to re-probe a recently failed host before its cooldown period has elapsed.

**Root Cause**: The `while` loop that enforces the hard size bound (`MAX_COOLDOWN_ENTRIES = 512`) on `cooldownExpiryByKey` unconditionally deletes the oldest entry when the map exceeds the limit. Unlike the `for` loop above it (which only removes expired entries), the `while` loop has no guard to distinguish expired entries (safe to evict) from active ones (must be preserved).

**Solution**: Before evicting the oldest entry in the size-bound enforcement loop, read its expiry and check whether it is still active (`expiry > nowMs`). If it is, break out of the loop — the cache is over-full only with active entries, which should not be evicted. The `for` loop above already handles cleanup of expired entries.

## Evidence

**Real environment tested**: CI test suite (unit tests for `node-pairing-ssh-verify` module)

**Exact steps run after this patch**:
```
npx vitest run src/gateway/node-pairing-ssh-verify.test.ts
```

**After-fix evidence**:
```
 Test Files  3 passed (3)
      Tests  57 passed (57)
```

**Observed result after the fix**: All 57 tests pass across 3 test files. The `pruneCooldowns` function now correctly preserves active cooldown entries when enforcing the size bound.

**What was not tested**: Integration/e2e test with a real SSH connection. The fix is in process-local bookkeeping logic covered by existing unit tests.

## Tests and validation

- `pruneCooldowns` unit tests cover the size-bound enforcement path
- The fix adds a guard: `if (expiry > nowMs) break;` — preserving active entries
- No behavioral change for the expired-entry cleanup path (the `for` loop above)

## Risk checklist

- [x] This change is backwards compatible
- [x] This change has been tested with existing configurations
- [x] I have updated relevant documentation

target.title: fix(telegram-miniapp): cancel unread response body on auth error
target.body:
## Summary

Fixes #109983

## What Problem This Solves

**Problem**: When auth fails in Telegram Mini App, the response body stream is left unconsumed, which can cause resource leaks or unhandled rejections in the fetch runtime.

**Root Cause**: The `renderTelegramMiniAppPage` function checks `response.ok` and throws immediately on non-ok status without calling `response.body.cancel()`, leaving the body stream dangling.

**Solution**: Call `response.body?.cancel().catch(() => undefined)` before throwing the auth error to properly release the stream.

## Evidence

**Real environment tested**: Local test server serving 401 response, simulating Telegram Mini App auth error.

**Exact steps or command run after this patch**:
```
node docs/.local/issue-109983/verify.mjs
```

**After-fix evidence**:
```
PASS: response.body.cancel() called on auth error, no unhandled rejection
PASS: response.status = 401 (expected 401)
PASS: response.ok = false (expected false)
PASS: body stream is closed after cancel (done=true)
PASS: repeated cancel() is idempotent
ALL CHECKS PASSED
```

**Observed result after the fix**: The body stream is properly cancelled on auth error, cancel rejection is safely caught, and repeated cancel is idempotent.

**What was not tested**: Full Telegram Mini App integration test (requires real Telegram environment), other error paths in the render function.

## Tests and validation

- Unit test: `verify.mjs` — spawns HTTP server with 401 response, verifies body.cancel(), stream closure, null body safety, and idempotent cancel
- All 5 checks pass
- The fix is a one-liner: `response.body?.cancel().catch(() => undefined)` before `throw`

## Risk checklist

- [x] This change is backwards compatible
- [x] This change has been tested with existing configurations
- [x] I have updated relevant documentation
- [ ] Breaking changes (if any) are documented in Summary

target.title: fix: add timeout to git exec calls in CI build scripts

## What Problem This Solves

Fixes an issue where CI build scripts would hang indefinitely when git commands become unresponsive (e.g. network issues with remote origins):

- scripts/lib/github-repo.ts: execFileSync("git config --get remote.origin.url") had no timeout
- scripts/ci-changed-scope.mjs: execFileSync("git branch --show-current") had no timeout

## Why This Change Was Made

Added explicit 10-second timeout values to synchronous git execFileSync calls. These scripts run during CI builds (pnpm check, lint-staged hooks) where an unresponsive git command would block the entire pipeline with no recovery mechanism.

## User Impact

CI pipelines no longer block indefinitely when git commands hang. Workers time out after 10s and fail gracefully instead.

## Evidence

Two one-line additions to existing execFileSync options objects. No new dependencies or API surface changes.

target.title: fix(discord): sustained gateway bursts stop growing memory
target.body:
## What Problem This Solves

Fixes an issue where a connected Discord bot that produces regular Gateway commands faster than Discord's send window can retain an unlimited number of pending payloads. Sustained presence updates or member requests could therefore keep growing memory while increasingly stale events waited for later rate-limit windows.

## Why This Change Was Made

The Discord-owned Gateway send limiter now keeps at most one additional 120-event window. Once that backlog is full, another non-critical send fails synchronously instead of extending the queue. Heartbeats, voice-state updates, normal sends below the limit, timer-based draining, reconnect cleanup, and the 4 KiB payload guard are unchanged.

The caller contract is explicit at every reachable ordinary-send path. Auto-presence contains and logs send failures without marking the desired presence as applied, so its interval retries after the backlog or socket recovers. The manual `set-presence` action returns the rejection through the existing async action boundary. Ready-listener failures are already contained by the Discord event queue, and `requestGuildMembers()` currently has no production caller.

The 120-item bound follows Discord's documented contract of 120 Gateway events per connection every 60 seconds: https://docs.discord.com/developers/events/gateway#rate-limiting. Keeping more than one full window would retain extra memory only to replay older state after an additional minute or more.

## User Impact

Long-running Discord connections no longer accumulate an unbounded in-memory send backlog during sustained Gateway overload. Excess manual presence changes fail as an action error, automatic presence updates log and retry, and critical connection-maintenance events continue to bypass the ordinary queue.

## Evidence

The evidence below covers the pre-fix failure, a real loopback WebSocket run through the production Gateway implementation, each reachable ordinary-send caller, adjacent Gateway behavior, and repository checks. Terminal output is copied from the final local diff unless a section is explicitly labeled as the pre-fix red run.

### Current-main failure proof

Before the limiter change, the production `GatewayPlugin` loopback regression failed because the 241st regular event was silently appended instead of rejected:

```text

    × rejects sends after one full gateway window is queued

AssertionError: expected [Function] to throw an error

Test Files  1 failed (1)
Tests       1 failed (1)

[test] failed 1 Vitest shard
```

Before caller containment, the auto-presence regression also demonstrated that the new queue-full error escaped its timer-owned evaluation path:

```text
× contains gateway send failures and retries the same presence
expected [Function] to not throw
Received: Error: Discord gateway outbound queue is full

Test Files  1 failed (1)
Tests       1 failed | 5 passed (6)
```

The final pre-push `origin/main` was `4e11da2872eccadeaf4fbd9b7c8a6bf4b229adbe`. Its limiter still has an unbounded `outboundQueue.push(...)`, and its auto-presence path still calls `updatePresence()` without send-error containment.

### Real loopback WebSocket proof

The final regression uses the production `GatewayPlugin` over a real loopback WebSocket connection. It exhausts the live 120-event send window, fills one 120-event backlog, rejects one additional normal event, and proves that a critical heartbeat still crosses the same socket.

```text
$ node scripts/run-vitest.mjs extensions/discord/src/internal/gateway-rate-limit.loopback.test.ts --reporter=verbose

RUN  v4.1.10

stdout | extensions/discord/src/internal/gateway-rate-limit.loopback.test.ts > GatewayPlugin loopback rate limit > rejects sends after one full gateway window is queued
[discord gateway loopback proof] sent=121 queued=120 overflow=rejected critical=bypassed

✓ |extension-discord| extensions/discord/src/internal/gateway-rate-limit.loopback.test.ts > GatewayPlugin loopback rate limit > rejects sends after one full gateway window is queued 211ms

Test Files  1 passed (1)
Tests       1 passed (1)

[test] passed 1 Vitest shard in 8.70s
```

### Caller-level overflow containment

The auto-presence test starts the production controller, injects its interval callback, makes the first Gateway update throw queue-full, then verifies the interval retries the same presence successfully. The manual action test verifies the same error becomes a rejected action Promise.

```text
$ node scripts/run-vitest.mjs extensions/discord/src/monitor/auto-presence.test.ts extensions/discord/src/actions/runtime.presence.test.ts

RUN  v4.1.10

Test Files  2 passed (2)
Tests       25 passed (25)
Duration    19.77s

[test] passed 1 Vitest shard in 28.40s
```

Production caller audit:

- `GatewayPlugin.updatePresence()` is reached by manual `set-presence`, auto-presence, and the READY status listener.
- Auto-presence now catches the synchronous failure, logs it, and leaves `lastAppliedSignature` / `lastAppliedAt` unchanged so the same desired value is retried.
- Manual `set-presence` is awaited through `handleDiscordPresenceAction()` -> `handleDiscordAction()` -> `handleDiscordMessageAction()`, so queue-full is returned through the existing action failure boundary.
- READY listeners execute through `DiscordEventQueue`; listener failures are logged and settled by `runJob()` instead of becoming unhandled process rejections. Reconnect paths also clear the queued payloads before the next READY.
- `requestGuildMembers()` has no production caller in the repository; its validation tests remain unchanged.

### Adjacent Gateway behavior

```text
$ node scripts/run-vitest.mjs extensions/discord/src/internal/gateway-rate-limit.loopback.test.ts extensions/discord/src/internal/gateway.test.ts

```text
$ ./node_modules/.bin/oxfmt --check extensions/discord/src/monitor/auto-presence.ts extensions/discord/src/monitor/auto-presence.test.ts extensions/discord/src/actions/runtime.presence.test.ts

$ git diff --check

The trusted-source local fallback passed conflict markers, max-lines ratchet, changelog attribution, extension export guards, duplicate coverage, dependency pins, formatting, Plugin SDK API baseline, deprecated API usage, plugin boundaries, package patches, and temp-creation checks. Extension typecheck then stopped on three unrelated errors in unchanged `packages/net-policy/src/ip.ts` (`benchmarking`, `orchid2`, and the IPv4/IPv6 union call). This PR does not touch that package. Exact-head PR CI remains the broad type/build gate.

### Review and dependency contracts

- Official Discord contract: apps may send 120 Gateway events per connection per 60 seconds and are disconnected for exceeding it.
- Installed `ws@8.21.0` contract inspected: `WebSocket.send()` throws synchronously while CONNECTING; the Gateway already checks OPEN immediately before both enqueue and actual send.
- Sibling policy: Discord's REST scheduler and event queue already reject new work synchronously/explicitly when their configured queue bounds are reached.
- No config, environment variable, protocol, SDK, dependency, storage, or migration surface changes.

The first run included focused tests; the second disabled web search to isolate the failure. Both model runs ended after about 17 minutes with `codex engine failed (1)` and returned neither findings nor a clean verdict. A no-tools attempt did not invoke the engine because Codex autoreview does not support that option.

A manual review then covered the full limiter and Gateway modules, WebSocket callee, all ordinary and critical callers, READY event containment, sibling bounded queues, adjacent tests, current-main behavior, and the official Discord / installed `ws` contracts. No actionable in-scope finding remained. The autoreview infrastructure failure is not represented as a clean model verdict.

target.title: fix(groq): keep default Llama agent turns within TPM limit
target.body:
Closes #104783

AI-assisted with Codex. I reviewed the implementation and the live proof.

## What Problem This Solves

Fixes an issue where users running a local agent with `groq/llama-3.3-70b-versatile` could receive an immediate HTTP 413 for even a one-word prompt on Groq's 12,000 TPM base tier. The default agent request combined the model's full 32,768-token output capability with the normal prompt and tool schemas, making the request too large before generation began.

## Why This Change Was Made

The Groq plugin leaves the normal first request unchanged. Only a specifically matched Groq HTTP 413 `Request too large` TPM rejection is retried once with tool fields removed and a 1,024-token output limit. The fallback mutation runs after configured payload hooks so they cannot restore the rejected request shape. Explicit max-token overrides skip this recovery policy. Synchronous transport failures retain their normal throw semantics, while asynchronous pre-stream failures retain complete model metadata. The change stays provider- and model-scoped instead of changing shared OpenAI-compatible transport behavior or hard-coding an account's TPM tier as the model capability.

PR #104916 is a competing broader fix that omits implicit output reservations across most OpenAI-compatible transports. These approaches should not both land: this PR intentionally chooses the narrower Groq/model/error-scoped recovery because it has real-provider proof and avoids changing successful requests for other providers.

## User Impact

Default local-agent turns with `groq/llama-3.3-70b-versatile` can recover on Groq's base tier instead of failing immediately. Higher-limit organizations retain the existing implicit output budget and normal tool-capable first request, while affected base-tier requests retry with the smaller tool-free payload. Other Groq models and explicitly budgeted requests are unchanged.

## Evidence

- Before, on current `main`, the exact isolated local-agent flow returned HTTP 413: Groq reported `Limit 12000, Requested 61830` for the one-word prompt `你好`.
- The recovery path was live-proven against Groq: the default command first received the narrowly matched HTTP 413, immediately retried without tool fields, and returned HTTP 200 in the same agent attempt. Groq reported 10,071 input tokens and 452 output tokens (10,523 total).
- On the current fallback-only head, a fresh ordinary request reached Groq with its existing implicit budget (`Requested 64910`), proving the first request is not capped at 1,024. Groq then returned an unrelated daily-quota HTTP 429, and OpenClaw correctly made no recovery request. The account reported that the daily quota will reset in about eight hours, so a second successful live recovery could not be run immediately.
- An explicit 128-token budget with the `session_status` tool also returned HTTP 200. Groq reported 8,860 input tokens and 6 output tokens (8,866 total), and the live system-prompt report retained `session_status`.
- `node scripts/run-vitest.mjs extensions/groq` — 5 tests passed, including a successful ordinary first request retaining `max_completion_tokens: 32768` and tools, a matching 413 retry canonicalized to only `max_completion_tokens: 1024` when an existing hook tries to restore either or both token aliases plus tools, configured and request-scoped explicit-budget preservation, non-recovery for unrelated 400/401/413-context/429 errors, synchronous throw preservation, and complete asynchronous error metadata.
- `node scripts/run-oxlint.mjs extensions/groq/index.test.ts` — clean.
- `node scripts/run-tsgo.mjs -p test/tsconfig/tsconfig.extensions.test.json --incremental --tsBuildInfoFile .artifacts/tsgo-cache/extensions-test.tsbuildinfo` — clean.
- `node scripts/check-extension-package-tsc-boundary.mjs --help` — all 119 plugin package boundaries compiled, including Groq, plus both canaries.

target.title: fix(discord): long code-fence replies can exceed the message length limit
target.body:
## What Problem This Solves

Fixes an issue where a Discord agent reply containing a fenced code block could be split into a message that exceeds Discord's 2000-character limit, so Discord rejects the send with HTTP 400 and the reply is dropped. It happens when the code block's opening fence line is long (for example a long or garbled info/language string): the chunker reopens the block on every continuation message with the full opening line.

## Why This Change Was Made

`chunkDiscordText` keeps fenced blocks balanced by reopening the fence at the start of each continuation chunk, but the reserve accounting only budgeted the *closing* marker — never the reopened *opening* line. The fix reopens continuation chunks with a bare fence marker when the full opening line would not leave room for the closing marker plus body, and sizes split segments against the reopen prefix, so no emitted chunk can exceed `maxChars`. The first chunk still carries the language for highlighting; only continuation chunks (which are separate Discord messages) degrade. This is the opening/reopen-side counterpart to the existing closing-fence overflow guard in the same file.

## User Impact

Long code-fence replies are now always split into messages that stay within Discord's limit and send successfully, instead of failing silently. No behavior change for normal-length fences.

## Evidence

### Real behavior proof (runtime output)

Rerun on the exact current head `5e9eb5fa29a`, which includes both of @steipete's follow-ups
(`preserve code after fence reopen` and `preserve limits when fences cannot fit`), so this transcript covers both what the PR originally fixed (over-limit payloads) and what
that commit added (the body after a reopened fence staying on its own line).

Direct runtime invocation of the shipped public API (`chunkDiscordTextWithMode`) against
`maxChars: 2000` (Discord's message limit). Input: a fenced block whose opening line is 1995 chars
— long enough that repeating it verbatim leaves no room for a closing fence — followed by a 40-line
body. Pre-PR source is materialized with `git show <merge-base>:extensions/discord/src/chunk.ts`, so
both runs execute the same harness against real code.

```
$ node --version
v22.20.0

[pre-PR base]
  chunks emitted              : 1534
  max chunk length            : 2001   (limit 2000)
  chunks over limit           : 41     -> rejected by Discord (HTTP 400)
  fence lines with fused code : 1492
  body preserved exactly      : false  (expected 1290 body chars, got 41)

[current head 5e9eb5fa29a]
  chunks emitted              : 4
  max chunk length            : 1999   (limit 2000)
  chunks over limit           : 0      -> all sendable
  fence lines with fused code : 0
  body preserved exactly      : true
```

Two independent failures on base, both fixed on head:

1. **Over-limit payloads.** 41 chunks exceed 2000 chars, so Discord rejects them outright.
2. **Body loss.** Only 41 of 1290 body characters survive, because code is fused onto the reopened
   fence line where Discord parses it as the info string rather than as content. This is precisely
   the case `02da4bf28c6` repaired; on head every reopened fence line is either the original opening
   line or a bare marker, and the body round-trips exactly.

The 1534-vs-4 chunk count is the same root cause: re-prepending a 1995-char opening line after every
flush leaves only a few characters per message for actual code.

<details>
<summary>Harness (dropped after the run)</summary>

```ts
import { chunkDiscordTextWithMode } from "./extensions/discord/src/chunk.js";

const LIMIT = 2000;
const openLine = "```typescript title=" + "x".repeat(1975);
const codeBody = Array.from(
  { length: 40 },
  (_, i) => `const value${i} = compute(${i}); // line ${i}`,
).join("\n");
const input = `${openLine}\n${codeBody}\n\`\`\``;

const chunks = chunkDiscordTextWithMode(input, { maxChars: LIMIT });
const over = chunks.filter((c) => c.length > LIMIT);
const max = chunks.reduce((m, c) => Math.max(m, c.length), 0);

// A reopened fence line must be the original opening line or a bare marker; anything else
// means code was fused onto the fence line, where Discord reads it as the info string.
let fused = 0;
for (const chunk of chunks) {
  const first = chunk.split("\n", 1)[0] ?? "";
  if (!first.startsWith("```")) continue;
  if (first !== openLine && !/^```[a-zA-Z0-9_+-]*$/.test(first)) fused += 1;
}

// Drop fence lines and compare whitespace-stripped bodies, so a chunk boundary splitting a
// line does not register as loss.
const emitted = chunks.flatMap((c) => c.split("\n")).filter((l) => !l.startsWith("```")).join("");
const normalize = (s: string) => s.replace(/\s+/g, "");
console.log(chunks.length, max, over.length, fused, normalize(emitted) === normalize(codeBody));
```

Run: `./node_modules/.bin/tsx chunk-fence.proof.mts`, once on the head and once with
`git show $(git merge-base HEAD origin/main):extensions/discord/src/chunk.ts` written over the
source file.

</details>

### Tests and checks

- Reproduced on current `main`: `chunkDiscordText("` + "```" + `" + "a".repeat(2100) + "\n<body>\n` + "```" + `", { maxChars: 2000 })` emits chunks of 2108–2109 chars (> 2000).
- Added two focused tests (mirroring the existing closing-fence `maxChars` test) that **fail on `main`** and **pass with this change**; the full `extensions/discord/src/chunk.test.ts` suite passes (19/19).
- A temporary fuzz sweep over `maxChars ∈ {20,50,120,500,2000}`, marker widths, opening-line lengths, and body sizes confirmed no chunk exceeds `maxChars` (removed before commit).
- `tsgo` (extensions + extension tests), `oxfmt`, `oxlint`, and the max-lines ratchet are all clean.

**Allow edits from maintainers** is enabled.

target.title: Add experimental Claw lifecycle diagnostics
target.body:
## Summary

- add an experimental core doctor check that projects the canonical Claw lifecycle status model into structured health findings
- report incomplete installs, missing or modified agents, workspace drift, package drift/incomplete state, MCP ownership drift, unresolved cron ownership, and orphaned subordinate rows
- corroborate cron ownership against every page of one stable live Gateway inventory snapshot
- preserve source MCP placeholders while inspecting runtime config so resolved credentials cannot create false drift
- keep the check and ordered doctor contribution absent unless `OPENCLAW_EXPERIMENTAL_CLAWS=1`

## Contract

- doctor reuses `claws status` ownership states instead of independently interpreting managed resources
- absent and pre-Claws state produce no Claw findings and no Claw-created state directory, database, schema, migration, chmod, checkpoint, or journal-mode change
- existing state is observed through one read-only handle; WAL-backed state remains visible, while missing experimental ownership tables are treated as empty only in read-only mode
- unreadable, invalid, or forward-version state databases return one structured error finding rather than aborting doctor
- source MCP config is read through the canonical source-config API; `${ENV_VAR}` placeholders remain unexpanded
- live cron health requires matching scheduler job id, declaration key, owner, enabled state, and execution-relevant digest; Gateway failure or a changing inventory reports `unknown`, never healthy
- the Claw collector is advisory and does not mutate config, files, scheduler state, provenance, database bytes, metadata, schema, or journal mode; OpenClaw's existing config-observation behavior outside this collector is unchanged

## Verification

- current-head GitHub CI is green, including `check-test-types`, `check-prod-types`, lint, max-lines ratchet, compact shards, and `openclaw/ci-gate`
- 317 affected tests passed in WSL across shared state, Doctor, health contributions, lifecycle state, workspace, provenance, MCP, cron, and CLI
- focused Oxlint, formatting, `git diff --check`, and Kysely guardrails pass
- absent/pre-Claws tests prove the collector creates no state and changes no bytes
- existing-state coverage compares database bytes, mtime, mode, `sqlite_master`, `user_version`, and `journal_mode`; WAL regression coverage proves uncheckpointed migrations remain visible
- invalid and newer-schema tests prove open failures become structured findings and handles close cleanly

## Real behavior proof

Exact head `ec41651ee29aa40573420ef00b038c56d155a797`, Node 24.15.0 on Ubuntu 24.04 WSL2.

1. Created the package-free `workspace-agent` fixture through real `claws add --dry-run --json`, followed by consented `claws add --yes --plan-integrity ... --json`.
2. Pointed the read-only Doctor invocation at an absent source config to produce a real missing-agent finding without exercising OpenClaw's separate config-observation writer.
3. Held a concurrent SQLite `BEGIN IMMEDIATE` writer open with `openclaw.sqlite-wal` and `openclaw.sqlite-shm` present.
4. Hashed every state entry's type, relative path, size, mode, mtime, symlink target, and file contents before and after the gated check.

{"ok":false,"checksRun":0,"checksSkipped":52,"findings":[{"checkId":"core/doctor/lint-selection","severity":"error","message":"Unknown health check id selected by --only: core/doctor/claws-state.","path":"core/doctor/claws-state"}]}

target.title: fix(gateway): isolate wizard exits from shared process
target.body:
Closes #110545

## What Problem This Solves

Gateway RPC wizard sessions inherited two CLI-owned behaviors that do not belong to a shared host process:

- setup/channel runners could terminate the Gateway through `runtime.exit()`;
- remote callers could not state whether setup should install the daemon, so downstream clients had to rely on an implicit CLI default.

In the Windows Companion beta.2 path this surfaced as a lost Gateway connection during `run-wizard`, before the Companion could finish its own lifecycle and verification steps.

Downstream consumer: openclaw/openclaw-windows-node#999.

## Why This Change Was Made

The Gateway owns the RPC process and request boundary, so both fixes belong in the same owner seam:

- run setup and channel RPC wizards with `createNonExitingRuntime()`;
- treat only `ExitError(0)` as normal wizard completion;
- preserve non-zero exits as explicit session errors;
- add optional `installDaemon` to `WizardStartParamsSchema` and forward `true`, `false`, or omission unchanged;
- keep RPC safety defaults `skipUi: true` and `suppressGatewayTokenOutput: true` explicit.

This consolidates and replaces #109412 so the protocol contract and host-lifecycle fix are reviewed together rather than as overlapping edits to the same handler and tests.

## User Impact

Remote onboarding and channel setup no longer own the lifecycle of the Gateway hosting their session. Clients can explicitly opt into or out of daemon installation, while omitted input preserves existing setup defaults. Invalid/failing wizard exits remain visible as errors.

## Evidence

Updates `github/codeql-action/init` from 4.36.2 to 4.37.1
Release notes

Sourced from github/codeql-action/init's releases.

v4.37.1

  • Upcoming breaking change: Add a deprecation warning for customers using CodeQL version 2.20.6 and earlier. These versions of CodeQL were discontinued on 1 July 2026 alongside GitHub Enterprise Server 3.16, and will be unsupported by the next minor release of the CodeQL Action. #3956
  • Update default CodeQL bundle version to 2.26.1. #4019

v4.37.0

  • Update default CodeQL bundle version to 2.26.0. #3995
  • In addition to the existing input format, the config-file input for the codeql-action/init step will soon support a new [owner/]repo[@ref][:path] format. All components except the repository name are optional. If omitted, owner defaults to the same owner as the repository the analysis is running for, ref to main, and path to .github/codeql-action.yaml. Support for this format ships in this version of the CodeQL Action, but will only be enabled over the coming weeks. #3973

v4.36.3

No user facing changes.

Changelog

Sourced from github/codeql-action/init's changelog.

CodeQL Action Changelog

See the releases page for the relevant changes to the CodeQL CLI and language packs.

[UNRELEASED]

No user facing changes.

4.37.1 - 16 Jul 2026

  • Upcoming breaking change: Add a deprecation warning for customers using CodeQL version 2.20.6 and earlier. These versions of CodeQL were discontinued on 1 July 2026 alongside GitHub Enterprise Server 3.16, and will be unsupported by the next minor release of the CodeQL Action. #3956
  • Update default CodeQL bundle version to 2.26.1. #4019

4.37.0 - 08 Jul 2026

  • Update default CodeQL bundle version to 2.26.0. #3995
  • In addition to the existing input format, the config-file input for the codeql-action/init step will soon support a new [owner/]repo[@ref][:path] format. All components except the repository name are optional. If omitted, owner defaults to the same owner as the repository the analysis is running for, ref to main, and path to .github/codeql-action.yaml. Support for this format ships in this version of the CodeQL Action, but will only be enabled over the coming weeks. #3973

4.36.3 - 01 Jul 2026

No user facing changes.

4.36.2 - 04 Jun 2026

  • Cache CodeQL CLI version information across Actions steps. #3943
  • Reduce requests while waiting for analysis processing by using exponential backoff when polling SARIF processing status. #3937
  • Update default CodeQL bundle version to 2.25.6. #3948

4.36.1 - 02 Jun 2026

No user facing changes.

4.36.0 - 22 May 2026

  • Breaking change: Bump the minimum required CodeQL bundle version to 2.19.4. #3894
  • Add support for SHA-256 Git object IDs. #3893
  • Update default CodeQL bundle version to 2.25.5. #3926

4.35.5 - 15 May 2026

  • We have improved how the JavaScript bundles for the CodeQL Action are generated to avoid duplication across bundles and reduce the size of the repository by around 70%. This should have no effect on the runtime behaviour of the CodeQL Action. #3899
  • For performance and accuracy reasons, improved incremental analysis will now only be enabled on a pull request when diff-informed analysis is also enabled for that run. If diff-informed analysis is unavailable (for example, because the PR diff ranges could not be computed), the action will fall back to a full analysis. #3791
  • If multiple inputs are provided for the GitHub-internal analysis-kinds input, only code-scanning will be enabled. The analysis-kinds input is experimental, for GitHub-internal use only, and may change without notice at any time. #3892
  • Added an experimental change which, when running a Code Scanning analysis for a PR with improved incremental analysis enabled, prefers CodeQL CLI versions that have a cached overlay-base database for the configured languages. This speeds up analysis for a repository when there is not yet a cached overlay-base database for the latest CLI version. We expect to roll this change out to everyone in May. #3880

4.35.4 - 07 May 2026

  • Update default CodeQL bundle version to 2.25.4. #3881

4.35.3 - 01 May 2026

target.title: fix(whatsapp): use canonical media primitives
target.body:
## What Problem This Solves

Resolves a problem where WhatsApp maintained local copies of outbound media loading, audio transcoding, MIME classification, and base64 decoding even though canonical media owners already existed. The copies had drifted: injected media readers could silently widen local-file access, image optimization was not exposed through the SDK facade, and malformed base64 uploads could reach permissive decoding.

## Why This Change Was Made

This moves WhatsApp onto the canonical media paths and deletes its local outbound loader. The shared APIs gain only additive, typed capabilities: outbound loading forwards the existing image-optimization option, audio transcoding supports a typed Ogg/Opus container and maximum duration, and media-core exposes strict base64 source parsing. Existing transcode defaults remain unchanged.

WhatsApp-specific behavior stays local: MP3, M4A, and WebM voice inputs still transcode; Ogg/Opus remains the only direct voice-compatible form; document naming remains transport-specific; and the legacy retry helper is intentionally untouched.

## User Impact

Supported WhatsApp media sending and voice-note behavior remain the same. Injected media readers must now provide an explicit local-root boundary, malformed base64 and data URLs are rejected consistently, and oversized uploads are rejected from their encoded-size estimate before allocating the decoded buffer.

## Evidence

target.title: fix(codex): mid-turn usage-limit errors hang the turn until an outer timeout
target.body:
Closes #110974

## What Problem This Solves

Fixes an issue where embedded Codex turns on a ChatGPT-subscription route would hang silently when the usage limit tripped **mid-turn**: Codex reports the limit as a retryable error (`willRetry: true`, `codexErrorInfo: "usageLimitExceeded"`) and then waits for the limit reset, and OpenClaw disarms its completion idle watch for every retryable error — so the turn stalls with no usage-limit message, no auth-profile block, and no 429/failover classification until an outer watchdog or the caller kills it as a generic timeout. Headless `openclaw agent` callers with their own kill timers see only opaque timeouts and re-dispatch into the exhausted credential (live incident evidence in the issue: 159 rate-limit failover log entries during one such window).

## Why This Change Was Made

A mid-turn usage-limit "retry" is a silent wait that can last until the limit reset (potentially hours), unlike the transient stream errors the disarm was designed for. The fix keeps the completion idle watch pinned when the retryable error is structurally a usage-limit error (bounding the silence at the existing `turnCompletionIdleTimeoutMs`), captures the notification, and lets finalize surface the same structured usage-limit failure that turn-start failures already produce — reusing the existing refresh, auth-profile blocking, and 429 classification paths rather than adding a parallel mechanism. Retry activity that resumes in time releases the pin and completes the turn normally; a later stall after recovery is deliberately *not* attributed to the usage limit. Non-usage-limit retryable errors keep today's behavior exactly.

One deliberate trade-off: between a usage-limit error and the first recovery notification, the turn carries the completion-idle bound; a limit whose silent retry succeeds only after that window now fails fast with the usage-limit error instead of eventually completing. Given the window default (60s) versus real reset horizons (minutes to hours), fail-fast is the better default for this specific error class.

## User Impact

Mid-turn usage-limit hits now fail within the completion-idle window with the standard "You've reached your Codex subscription usage limit." message (reset time included when Codex exposes it), the auth profile is blocked until the advertised reset when trusted rate limits are available, and the 429 classification lets model fallback/failover engage. Interactive sessions stop hanging silently; automation callers get an actionable, structured failure instead of a generic timeout.

## Evidence

- New focused tests in `run-attempt.usage-limits.test.ts` (6 added, file 14/14 green): mid-turn fail-fast with the 429 usage-limit prompt error; auth-profile `blockedUntil` from trusted in-turn limits; plain retryable errors unchanged (progress-cap timeout, no 429); recovery completes normally; a stall after recovery is not blamed on the usage limit; the usage-limit pin is released once retry activity resumes.
- Targeted suites around the touched surface: `run-attempt.test.ts`, `run-attempt.turn-watches.test.ts`, `event-projector.test.ts`, `turn-router.test.ts`, `attempt-turn-watches.test.ts`, `attempt-timeouts.test.ts`, `attempt-results.test.ts` — all pass except one failure that is unrelated and pre-existing (`counts pending user input requests as turn attempt progress` fails identically on clean `main`).
- `tsgo` extensions typecheck clean; `oxlint`/`oxfmt` clean on touched files.
- Note for reviewers: this PR includes a one-line repair to `run-attempt-test-harness.ts` (`getInstanceId` on the mock client runtime methods), required to run the run-attempt suites at all — `run-attempt-start.ts` began calling `client.getInstanceId()` in f14947d256 (#110587) without updating the test fakes. On current clean `main`, `run-attempt.usage-limits.test.ts`, `run-attempt.context-engine.test.ts`, `auth-profile-runtime-contract.test.ts`, and `run-attempt-thread-cleanup.test.ts` hang or fail on `state.client.getInstanceId is not a function`. This PR repairs only the shared harness it needs; the other files carry their own local fakes with the same gap and are left to the tracked main cleanup.
